## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- **Define** data ethics and **explain** why it goes beyond legal compliance and technical correctness. *(Understand)*
- **Explain** algorithmic bias -- where it comes from -- and **why** fairness is contested (different fairness criteria can conflict). *(Understand / Analyze)*
- **Explain** privacy, the limits of informed consent, and **how** re-identification defeats "anonymous" data. *(Understand / Analyze)*
- **Analyze** a data scenario for its ethical stakes with a simple principle framework, and **take and defend** a position. *(Analyze / Evaluate)*

> **Where this sits:** **Unit VII** closed the technical arc (graphs and communities) · this lesson opens **Unit VIII -- Governance** and turns the course's question from *can we?* to *should we?* · it cashes in the **fairness caveat flagged in L15** · **L28** follows with the *law* that codifies some of these duties.

## Why This Matters

Every technique in this course is **dual-use**. The recommender that surfaces a film you love (Unit VI)
is the same machinery that can trap someone in a filter bubble. The community detection that finds your
study group (Unit VII) is the same method that can map a protest network. The classifier you built in
**L15** to predict income from census features could, with different labels, decide who gets a loan, a
job interview, or bail. And every one of these began the same way -- data **acquired** from real people
(L06) and **turned into features** (L11-L12), people who are rarely in the room when the model is built
and never see the decision it makes about them.

The methods do not arrive with ethics attached -- that part is yours. And the accuracy score, the metric
you have optimized all semester, is silent on the questions that matter most here:

- **Who is harmed when the model is wrong -- and wrong about *whom*?**
- **Whose data is this, and did they agree to *this* use of it?**
- **What power does this system hand to whom?**

**Data ethics** is the discipline of asking those questions *in time* -- before the system ships, not
after the harm. This lesson works through three tensions where they most often go unasked, each anchored
in a real case you can look up, and gives you a framework for reasoning about the next one.

## What Is Data Ethics?

**Ethics** is about what we *should* do -- it is distinct from two things it is easily confused with:

- It is **not the same as the law.** The law is the floor (and the subject of L28); plenty that is legal
  is still wrong, and the law always lags the technology. Ethics asks what you should do even where no
  statute reaches.
- It is **not the same as accuracy.** A model can be technically excellent -- high accuracy, clean code,
  reproducible -- and still cause harm, violate consent, or entrench a power imbalance.

Data work carries unusual ethical weight for three reasons: **scale** (a single model can touch
millions), **opacity** (those affected often cannot see, question, or appeal the decision), and
**consequence** (the outputs decide loans, jobs, bail, and what billions of people see). With that reach
comes responsibility.

## Theme 1 -- Bias and Fairness

A model learns patterns from data. If the data, the labels, or the world they came from are biased, the
model learns the bias -- and then applies it at scale, with a veneer of mathematical objectivity.

**Where bias enters** is rarely the algorithm itself; it is the pipeline around it:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[The world<br/>historical inequity] --> B[Training data<br/>who is sampled, who is missing]
    B --> C[Labels<br/>what 'good' was defined as]
    C --> D[Model<br/>learns the pattern]
    D --> E[Decisions<br/>applied at scale]
    E -->|feedback loop| B
```

- **Biased data:** if a group is under-represented or recorded differently, the model serves it worse.
- **Biased labels:** the target itself can encode human prejudice -- "was re-arrested" is not "committed a
  crime", it is "was policed and caught", which differs by neighbourhood.
- **Feedback loops:** a model's decisions shape the next round of data (predictive policing sends officers
  where it predicted crime, which generates more recorded crime *there*, which confirms the prediction).

Three documented cases:

> - **COMPAS** (ProPublica, *Machine Bias*, 2016) -- a widely used recidivism risk score was found to
>   produce racially disparate error rates: Black defendants who did not re-offend were flagged high-risk
>   far more often than white defendants who did not re-offend.
> - **Gender Shades** (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018) -- commercial face-classification systems were far less
>   accurate on darker-skinned women than on lighter-skinned men, because the benchmark data was skewed.
> - **Amazon's recruiting tool** (2018, scrapped) -- trained on a decade of mostly-male resumes, it learned
>   to down-rank resumes that contained the word "women's" (as in "women's chess club captain").

**Fairness is contested.** There is no single definition. Should a model have equal *error rates* across
groups, or equal *positive-prediction rates*, or treat *similar individuals* similarly? These sound
compatible but are not: when base rates differ between groups, it is mathematically impossible to satisfy
several reasonable fairness criteria at once (this was the core of the COMPAS debate). "Make it fair" is
therefore not a setting you toggle -- it is a value judgment about *which* fairness you mean, made in the
open, with the affected people in mind.

> **The L15 callback.** In the data-mining mini-project you trained a classifier on census data to predict
> income, and we flagged that its predictions are *associational* and *fairness-laden*. Now you can name
> why: the features (occupation, hours, education) correlate with protected attributes, the label reflects
> a historically unequal economy, and "accurate" says nothing about "fair". That flag was pointing here.

## Theme 2 -- Privacy and Consent

**Privacy** is not secrecy; it is *control over information about yourself*. Two ideas do most of the work:

- **Informed consent and its limits.** The ethical default is that people agree to how their data is used.
  But consent at data scale is thin: nobody reads the terms, "I agree" is a precondition of using the
  service, and no checkbox can anticipate every *future* use of data collected today. Real consent is
  specific and revocable; most data consent is neither.
- **Re-identification: anonymization is not deletion.** Stripping names does not make data anonymous,
  because *combinations* of ordinary attributes are unique, and separate datasets can be *linked*.

> - **Netflix Prize de-anonymization** (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008) -- Netflix released 100M "anonymous"
>   movie ratings for a contest; researchers re-identified users by matching rating patterns to public
>   IMDb reviews.
> - **Latanya Sweeney** showed that **ZIP code + birth date + sex** uniquely identifies a large share of
>   the US population, and used it to pull the Governor of Massachusetts's medical record out of an
>   "anonymized" hospital release -- the work that motivated *k*-anonymity.
> - **The AOL search-log release** (2006) -- "anonymized" search histories were published; journalists
>   identified individuals from the content of their own queries within days.

The lesson: **aggregation and linkage defeat naive anonymization.** Collecting less, and assuming any
release can be linked, is safer than trusting that removing names is enough.

## Theme 3 -- Surveillance and Power

Data is **power**, and it is usually *asymmetric*: the organization sees the individual in fine detail,
while the individual cannot see, question, or opt out of the organization. Scaled up, routine data
collection becomes **surveillance** -- and surveillance shapes behaviour (people self-censor when watched)
and concentrates power.

> - **Cambridge Analytica / Facebook** (2018) -- the data of tens of millions of users was harvested
>   through a personality quiz (and their friends' data, without those friends' knowledge) and used to
>   build profiles for political ad targeting -- consent that was meaningless at the point it mattered.
> - **"Surveillance capitalism"** (Zuboff, named) describes a business model in which human experience is
>   raw material for behavioural prediction; **predictive policing** turns past enforcement into future
>   suspicion. Both are power-asymmetry stories before they are technology stories.

## A Framework for Reasoning

You will not memorize the right answer to every case -- there isn't one. Instead, carry a small set of
principles and run them on each project. A compact, widely used set:

- **Respect for persons** -- people are not just data points; consent and autonomy matter.
- **Beneficence** -- maximize benefit, minimize harm; ask who bears each.
- **Justice** -- distribute benefits and harms fairly; watch who is made worse off.
- **Transparency and accountability** -- can the decision be explained, contested, and owned by someone?

Two lenses help when principles tension: a **consequences** lens (what outcomes does this produce, for
whom?) and a **duties** lens (what do we owe these people regardless of outcome?). When they disagree, you
have found the hard part of the problem -- name it rather than hide it.

A four-question checklist for any data project:

1. **Whose data is this, and did they meaningfully agree to this use?**
2. **Who is harmed if the system is wrong -- and is that harm spread evenly?**
3. **Could the outputs be re-identified, linked, or repurposed beyond the intent?**
4. **Who gains power from this system, and who can contest its decisions?**

## Your Responsibility

Ethics is **part of the job**, not a compliance box checked at the end by someone else. The data scientist
is often the only person who understands *how* the system actually works, which makes you the person best
positioned -- and obligated -- to raise the hard question early. Concretely: ask these questions at design
time, **document** the data's provenance and the model's known limits, build in ways to **audit and
contest** decisions, and be willing to **push back** on a use you cannot defend. "I just built the model"
is not a place to stand.

> **Forward to L28.** Some of these duties are now **law**. The next lesson covers the regulations and
> standards that codify privacy, consent, and accountability -- GDPR, HIPAA, FERPA, and the Puerto Rico /
> US context -- and how to apply one to a real data-handling scenario. Ethics is what you should do; law is
> where society made part of it mandatory.

## Discussion Prompts

No single right answer -- argue from the framework, and say which principle you are weighing.

1. **Bias.** A bank's loan model is more accurate overall when it *includes* ZIP code, but ZIP code
   correlates strongly with race. Drop it (and lose accuracy) or keep it (and risk a discriminatory
   proxy)? What would you need to know to decide?
2. **Privacy.** A university wants to predict which students will drop out, using login logs, card swipes,
   and grades, to offer help early. Helpful intervention or unconsented surveillance? What would make it
   ethical?
3. **Consent / public data.** Researchers scrape millions of *public* social-media profiles to study
   mental health. The data is public -- does that make any use of it fair? Who should have a say?
4. **Power.** A city deploys predictive policing trained on historical arrest data. Trace the feedback
   loop. Who benefits, who is harmed, and who can contest a patrol decision?

## FAQ

**Isn't following the law enough?**
No. The law is the floor and it lags the technology; much that is legal is still harmful or unjust. Ethics
asks what you should do, including where no law yet reaches. (L28 covers what the law *does* require.)

**If the data is public, is it fair game for any use?**
Not automatically. People share in one context expecting one use; harvesting it at scale for a different
purpose (profiling, training, re-identification) can violate the reasonable expectation under which it was
shared. "Public" is about access, not consent to every downstream use.

**Can't we just remove the sensitive attribute (race, sex) to make the model fair?**
No -- this is "fairness through unawareness", and it usually fails. Other features act as **proxies** (ZIP
code for race, first name for sex), so the model reconstructs the attribute and the disparity persists,
now harder to detect. Fairness requires measuring outcomes across groups, not hiding the variable.

**Whose job is the ethics -- isn't there a compliance team for that?**
Compliance handles the legal minimum after the fact. The person who built the system understands it best
and is best placed to catch problems at design time. Ethics is shared, but it is not someone else's
problem.

## Where to Go Deeper

- **ProPublica, "Machine Bias" (2016)** -- the COMPAS investigation, with the data and methodology.
- **Buolamwini & Gebru, "Gender Shades" (2018)** -- the facial-analysis accuracy audit (gendershades.org).
- **Cathy O'Neil, *Weapons of Math Destruction* (2016)** -- accessible cases of harmful models at scale.
- **Barocas, Hardt & Narayanan, *Fairness and Machine Learning*** -- the standard text, free at
  fairmlbook.org (start with the introduction and the chapter on classification).
- **The Belmont Report (1979)** -- the origin of the respect / beneficence / justice principles, written
  for human-subjects research and still the backbone of data ethics.
